faq.a: It is the imaginary line Earth spins around, passing through the North and South Poles. It is tilted about 23.4 degrees and points almost exactly at the North Star.

faq.q: Why do the stars circle around the sky?
faq.a: Because Earth is spinning. As we turn, the whole sky appears to rotate the opposite way around the points above the poles. Near the North Star, stars trace small circles; further away, they rise and set.
asks: Why do stars move in circles in photos?

faq.q: Which star is the North Star?
faq.a: Polaris, in the constellation of the Little Bear. You can find it by following the two end stars of the Plough's bowl, also called the Big Dipper, which point towards it.

faq.q: How did sailors use the North Star?
faq.a: Because Polaris always marks north, sailors could steer by it at night. Measuring its height above the horizon also told them their latitude, how far north they were.
asks: How does the North Star help you navigate?

faq.q: Is the North Star the brightest star?
faq.a: No. Polaris is only around the 48th brightest star in the sky; the brightest is Sirius. Polaris is famous for its position, not its brightness.
asks: Is Polaris the brightest star in the sky?

facts: Polaris lies less than 1 degree from the north celestial pole.
Because Earth's axis slowly wobbles over about 26,000 years, the pole star changes; Vega will be near the pole in about 12,000 years.
The southern hemisphere has no bright pole star.

quiz.why: Polaris sits less than a degree from the point the axis points to, so as Earth spins it hardly moves.

wrong.0: The closest star is the Sun, then Proxima Centauri; Polaris is hundreds of light years away.
wrong.2: Its stillness comes from its position above the axis, not its speed.
